title: What Self-Adhesive Cable Clips Are
description: Self-adhesive cable clips are small plastic or silicone holders with a sticky backing — press one to the desk edge or case, lay the cable in its channel, and the cable stays routed. Drop holders (like the BlueLounge-style) weight cables at the desk edge so they do not slide off. They are the anchoring half of cable management: straps bundle, clips anchor.

print("Clip: sticky backing + cable channel = cable stays routed.")
print("Drop holder: weighted, parks cable at desk edge (no slide-off).")
print("Straps BUNDLE, clips ANCHOR: the two halves of cable management.")

t: How the Adhesive Works (and Its Limits)
title: How the Adhesive Works (and Its Limits)
description: Most clips use 3M-style acrylic foam adhesive: strong on clean flat surfaces, removable with heat and patience. The bond needs 24 hours to reach full strength — clip today, load tomorrow. Limits: textured surfaces, dusty surfaces, and heat (near radiators) all weaken it. Clean with IPA, press firmly for 30 seconds, wait a day: the ritual that makes adhesive trustworthy.

demo.program:
print("3M-style acrylic foam: strong on CLEAN FLAT surfaces.")
print("Full strength at 24h: clip today, load tomorrow.")
print("Weakens: texture, dust, heat. Ritual: IPA clean + 30s press + 1 day wait.")

title: Clip Sizes and Cable Counts
description: Clips come single-channel (one cable each — cleanest look) and multi-channel (3-5 cables per clip — fewer clips, busier look). Size the channel to the cable: a USB-C cable in an oversized clip slides; in a tight clip it seats. For desk edges, single clips spaced 6-8 inches give the tidiest runs; multi-clips suit the hidden back edge where looks do not matter.

demo.program:
print("Single-channel: one cable each, cleanest look, spaced 6-8 in on desk edge.")
print("Multi-channel (3-5): fewer clips, busier. Hidden back edge is fine.")
print("Channel ~= cable diameter: oversized slides, tight seats.")

title: Placement Strategy: The Desk-Edge Run
description: The canonical desk run: clips along the desk's back edge every 6-8 inches, cables dropping from monitors and peripherals into the clips, then into the under-desk tray or sleeve. Keep power left and data right (or vice versa — just be consistent). The first clip sits where cables leave the monitor; the last where they enter the tray. Plan the path before sticking anything.

demo.program:
print("Path: monitor -> clips every 6-8 in along back edge -> tray/sleeve.")
print("Power one side, data other (consistent!).")
print("PLAN the path first: stuck clips move, but adhesive weakens each move.")

title: Use Case: Anchoring Sleeved Trunks
description: Sleeved trunks need anchors at both ends or they migrate — clips at the desk edge and where the trunk meets the PC pin it in place. The clip's channel should fit the sleeved diameter (bigger than the bare cables). Two clips minimum per trunk; long runs get one every 2 feet. Anchored trunks stay where the routing planned them.

t: Use Case: Inside the Case (With Caveats)
title: Use Case: Inside the Case (With Caveats)
description: Adhesive clips work inside cases for light routing — fan cables along the shroud, LED strips — but heat softens adhesive over time, so case clips are semi-permanent at best. For structural anchoring inside cases, prefer screw-mount ties. Clips are for light, cool, low-vibration spots; anything structural gets a mechanical mount.

title: Removing Clips Without Damage
description: Removal: heat the clip with a hair dryer for 30 seconds to soften the adhesive, then peel slowly while pulling the adhesive foam (stretch it — 3M foam releases when stretched). Residue comes off with IPA or adhesive remover. Rushing the peel pulls paint and finish; heat plus patience leaves the surface clean. The 24-hour cure that made it strong yields to heat.

demo.program:
print("Heat 30s (hair dryer) -> peel SLOW, stretch the foam (releases).")
print("Residue: IPA / adhesive remover. Rushing pulls paint: heat + patience.")
print("The cure that made it strong yields to heat.")

title: Clip Materials: Plastic vs Silicone
description: Hard plastic clips hold shape and grip firmly — best for fixed runs. Silicone clips flex, grip gently, and suit cables you plug/unplug often (chargers, headphones). Metal clips exist for industrial heat. For desks: silicone at the edge (frequent handling), plastic along the back (fixed runs). Match flex to handling frequency.

print("Metal: industrial heat. Match flex to handling frequency.")

title: Clips vs Raceways vs Trays
description: Clips: cheapest, most flexible, one cable at a time — best for edges and light runs. Raceways (adhesive channels): hide a whole bundle in one covered strip — cleaner look, harder to change. Trays: hold power bricks and bulk under the desk — the heavy-duty answer. The desk system usually combines all three: clips route, raceway hides, tray holds.

print("raceways : covered strip, clean, harder to change. Hide the bundle.")
print("trays    : power bricks + bulk under desk. Heavy duty.")
print("System: clips route, raceway hides, tray holds.")

t: Buying Guide: Adhesive Quality Is Everything
title: Buying Guide: Adhesive Quality Is Everything
description: The clip is plastic; the product is the adhesive. Buy clips with genuine 3M adhesive — no-name foam fails in months, especially with any warmth. A 20-60 pack costs 8-12 dollars; you will use more than you think. Test one clip for a week before committing to a full run: adhesive that survives your desk's temperature survives the job.

t: Common Mistakes: Overloading and Wrong Surfaces
title: Common Mistakes: Overloading and Wrong Surfaces
description: The classic failures: five cables in a two-cable clip (they pop out), clips on dusty textured surfaces (they fall in days), loading before the 24-hour cure (they slide), and clipping hot cables near radiators (adhesive cooks). Each is a planning failure, not a product failure — the clip works when the surface, count, cure, and temperature are right.

demo.program:
print("Fails: overloading | dusty/textured surface | loading before 24h cure | heat.")
print("Each = planning failure, not product failure.")
print("Right surface + right count + full cure + cool = clips that last years.")
